title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
titleJa: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
summaryJa: The American-made interceptors are the only effective weapon for downing Russia's ballistic missiles.
bodyOriginal:
US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
- Published
The United States has approved the sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically-needed munition for defence against escalating Russian aerial attacks.
However Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has warned it could take "several years" for the deliveries to arrive.
The US State Department said the advanced PAC-3 interceptor missiles would cost $2.1bn (£1.6bn) and would be "funded entirely" by Kyiv's allies in Europe and Canada.
On Friday night Zelensky repeated his calls for the US to speed up the release of its Patriots - the only effective weapon in downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles.
Hundreds evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky during rare Ukraine ceasefire
- Published12 hours ago
G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
- Published7 hours ago
The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel.
The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east.
Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.
In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".
It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan".
The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".
Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.
The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.
Zelensky said earlier this week that Ukraine had been waiting almost a month for the US to sign off on critical missile supplies which his country was running critically low on.
In a post on X late on Friday, he welcomed the US announcement but said Ukraine needed the Patriot missiles "right now".
He said Russia was intensifying its attacks on key energy infrastructure ahead of winter with "more than 30 Russian strikes" on "critical parts" of Ukraine's power grid over the past two weeks.
Kyiv desperately needs the interceptors but there is a global shortage of the munitions due to their use by the US in its war against Iran.
It is not clear what the production schedule will be for the Patriots - but it is understood the order is for new builds rather than existing missiles, meaning there is unlikely to be any kind of rapid delivery to Ukraine.
Patriots also have lengthy production times, with only 600 missiles produced per year according to the US Department of Defence.
In July, Trump said Washington had "not agreed" to license Ukraine to produce Patriots - three weeks after offering the country such a right.
Additional reporting by Victoria Bourne

title: Alaska Senate election: DOJ wants to 'segregate' all ballots for 2nd Sullivan candidate
titleJa: Alaska Senate election: DOJ wants to 'segregate' all ballots for 2nd Sullivan candidate
summaryJa: The winner of the Alaska election could determine whether Republicans retain their majority in the U.S. Senate or if Democrats take control of the chamber.
bodyOriginal:
The Department of Justice wants "to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking" a candidate named Dan Sullivan for a potential investigation of whether voters in Alaska's U.S. Senate election mistakenly ranked him in the belief he was incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, a federal prosecutor told a judge in a court filing late Friday.
The filing came in a lawsuit by the DOJ, which asks District Court Judge Sharon Gleason to block state election officials from immediately certifying the Senate election if Sen. Sullivan loses by a margin that might be attributable to voter confusion from the presence of the other Sullivan on the ballot. The DOJ wants to conduct an investigation to determine voter intent if the incumbent loses.
"Election Day is on November 3, 2026, which poses a substantial risk that the candidacy before us will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity," U.S. Attorney for Alaska Michael Heyman said in the filing, signed by one of his assistant prosecutors.
"The United States of America contends that the proposed precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, showing good cause for expedited consideration," the filing said.
Heyman earlier Friday told reporters at a press conference that there is an "ongoing" criminal investigation into how and why retired school teacher Dan Sullivan decided to run for the Senate for the first time this year.
The DOJ's suit, which President Donald Trump said he had requested, claims the "sole purpose" of the non-incumbent Sullivan running was to benefit the campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola by reducing the number of votes for Sen. Sullivan.
"We will not let anyone or any group undermine this election," said Heyman at a press conference in Anchorage, which was held just four days before Election Day.
"There is both a civil investigation and a criminal investigation that is ongoing," Heyman said. "There is a surge of FBI resources and resources in this office."
"Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they're going to get one," the prosecutor said.
He said that the criminal probe has been underway for months. Heyman had previously recused himself from the probe because he was being considered for a judicial nomination, but that recusal was rescinded Thursday because he was no longer under consideration.
Heyman said the criminal investigation has been accelerated because of a New York Times report on Wednesday that said aides Peltola's campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee helped recruit the retired teacher to enter the Senate race with the hope of drawing votes from the incumbent Sullivan.
"When credible information comes out, we are committed to pursuing that information … and we will act on it," Heyman said.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC deny being involved in the retiree's Senate campaign.
Heyman, when questioned by reporters, would not say what criminal statute might have been violated
Earlier Friday, a federal judge kept on a fast track efforts to dismiss the DOJ's suit.
Judge Sharon Gleason ordered the DOJ to respond by 1 p.m. Alaska Time to the new dismissal motions, which were filed hours after the department amended its suit in U.S. District Court in Anchorage on Thursday to add a new legal claim.
The DOJ's updating of the civil complaint forced Gleason to rule the prior dismissal motions were moot.
Gleason gave state election officials, the campaign of Democratic nominee and other groups until noon Saturday to reply to the DOJ's response.
The judge's order leaves open the possibility that she will rule on the dismissal motions before Tuesday, which is Election Day, as both the state and Peltola's campaign have requested.
The state, the campaign, and other intervenors in the suit argue the DOJ has no legal authority to block certification of an election because two candidates on a four-candidate ballot happen to share the same name.
The winner of Alaska's race could determine which party holds a majority in the Senate starting in January. Republicans currently have 53 seats in the 100-member chamber.
Alaska's election uses ranked-choice voting. If no candidate obtains more than 50% of the vote in the first count, then the fourth-place finisher will be eliminated, and the second choice on that candidate's ballots will be allocated to the remaining candidates.
Only Peltola and Sen. Sullivan are considered likely to draw large shares of the votes.
The DOJ's suit seeks to delay certification of the Senate election if Sen. Sullivan loses by a margin that could be attributable to voter confusion over the presence of the other candidate, who is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan, on the ballot.
The amended complaint, which updates the suit filed Oct. 23, added a claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution to the first claim, under the National Voter Registration Act.
It also contained added details from the Times article.
Peltola's campaign, in its dismissal motion filed Thursday, said, "Rather than defend its indefensible legal claims as it was ordered to do, the Department of Justice ... has filed an Amended Complaint that does nothing to address the fatal problems that preclude it from bringing this case or obtaining the relief that it seeks."
"The U.S. Constitution leaves the regulation of federal elections exclusively to the States and to Congress, and DOJ has no statutory authority to bring this case," the motion said.
In their own dismissal motion, state election officials said the amended lawsuit "rests on the same meritless theory that the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) — a voter registration law — governs this case, which has nothing to do with voter registration."
"Because this reading of the NVRA fails, the amended complaint fails," the motion said.

title: Meta outlook revised downward by S&P on cash flow and capex concerns
titleJa: Meta outlook revised downward by S&P on cash flow and capex concerns
summaryJa: Meta has been given a negative outlook by S&P Global Ratings due to the company's hefty capital expenditures and concerns about free cash flow.
bodyOriginal:
Meta's outlook has been revised downward by S&P Global Ratings on concerns surrounding cash flow and AI spending.
The credit agency said Friday that the outlook reflects "uncertainty" about Meta's elevated capex and its negative free cash flow.
Meta's credit rating was revised from AA- stable to AA- negative, S&P said. S&Ps highest credit rating is AAA. Anything below BBB falls into the junk bond category.
The agency questioned "Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments" relative to its peers, which are also spending heavily on data center buildouts and going cash flow negative in the process.
Although Meta has recently debuted its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, S&P said "it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years."
A Meta spokesperson pushed back on the revision.
"We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," the spokesperson said in a statement. "We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile."
Meta said in its third-quarter earnings report last week that it expects full-year capex to come in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, going in the red for the first time.
Investors sent Meta shares down 7% following the report despite a revenue beat. The stock finished October down 15%, its worst month in four years.
The company said on Monday that it plans to raise $95 billion to help fund its AI initiatives, with plans to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program.
S&P said that while it expects Meta's capex growth to start "flattening out beginning in 2028," the agency is "less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated."

title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
titleJa: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
summaryJa: The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind.
bodyOriginal:
Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea
- Published
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.
The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.
The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.
America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.
While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.
The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
- Published10 hours ago
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."
Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate".
Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach.
In a later update, the firm set it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens.
The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York.
Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.
But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling.
It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.
Related topics
- Published26 August

summaryJa: Shares in Intel continue to fall while the tech-heavy Nasdaq opens at its lowest level in more than two months.
bodyOriginal:
US tech stocks see sharp falls as AI spending nears $1tn
- Published
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).
Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.
Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.
While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.
Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.
Alphabet's stock market value fell sharply on Thursday, taking more than $500bn (£374bn) off its market value after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.
At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.
The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.
The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.
On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.
"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.
In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.
Amazon and Reddit down
Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.
The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.
Amazon shares recovered some overnight losses, but were still down by 1.4% at the end of Friday trading.
Reddit stock plunged by 29%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.
Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by 18%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.
Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.
Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.
He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".
"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."
'Investors have turned ruthless'
Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market.
The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it.
Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months.
"Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said.
"The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs."
However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago.
While the Nasdaq closed 2.8% lower, it is up 7.8% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 8% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.3%.
Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks.
"If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

title: Intel stock has worst day since 1970s, wiping about $12 billion off government's stake
titleJa: Intel stock has worst day since 1970s, wiping about $12 billion off government's stake
summaryJa: Investors are nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether that will pay off.
bodyOriginal:
Intel shares plummeted 29% on Friday, their worst day since the 1970s, after the chipmaker issued weaker-than-expected guidance due to a plant shutdown in Israel and ongoing softness in the PC market.
It's a major setback for CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who was hired in March 2025, and has since been on a campaign to revive the company after it missed out on the early years of the artificial intelligence boom.
Intel's plunge is also a big hit to the Trump administration, which led the U.S. government into taking a 10% stake in the company over a year ago. While it's still a profitable investment, the value of those holdings dropped by about $12 billion on Friday. Nvidia also took a big stake in Intel, and its stock dropped by about $6 billion in value.
Heading into Thursday's earnings report, Intel shares were up about 150% this year, buoyed by demand for central processors, which are becoming critical to agentic AI workloads. Analysts at D.A. Davidson downgraded the stock to neutral from buy on Friday in a report titled, "Not fixed yet."
"We understand the PC market is being impacted at the industry level," the analysts wrote. "However it is hard to justify the current multiple when weakness is so significant."
Amazon shares also sold off on Friday, slipping 1.4%, after the company reported a third-quarter miss on the top and bottom line while maintaining its capital expenditure forecast for 2026 of $220 billion. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, and a big increase from the previous period.
The Nasdaq Composite slid 2.9%, capping off a week of rough tech earnings. Alphabet on Thursday suffered its worst day on record, plunging more than 12%. The stock fell again on Friday.
Other semiconductor names also notched declines. Chip giant Nvidia fell 4%, while Broadcom dropped more than 5% and mobile chipmaker Qualcomm tumbled 11%.
Not a 'moment of reckoning'
Investors are growing nervous about the massive AI spending from the tech giants and whether their investments will pay off.
"I don't think this is a moment of reckoning but I think it's a moment where investors should take a long thought about how positioning across the space still remains crowded even though the fundamentals are strong," Matt Orton, chief market strategist at Raymond James, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday.
For Intel, the disappointing forecast reflects a PC market that's getting hammered due to soaring costs for memory and other components. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research.
Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents this quarter on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG.
"We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel finance chief David Zinsner, said in the release. "We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth."
The guidance also accounts for the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said.
Tan said the explosion, which he called an "unfortunate and tragic accident," caused an "extended shutdown" at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips.
Key to Tan's turnaround effort is Intel's foundry business, which has struggled to find its footing.
Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Its next Arizona fab is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028.
Intel still has no external customers for its new chips.
"We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters," Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making "tremendous progress" on its coming 14A chips.

title: Reid Hoffman gives millions to Dems in late spending spree as Epstein fight spills into election
titleJa: Reid Hoffman gives millions to Dems in late spending spree as Epstein fight spills into election
summaryJa: Reid Hoffman has given $8 million to Wisconsin Democrats backing David Crowley as Tom Tiffany attacks Hoffman's past ties to Jeffrey Epstein.
bodyOriginal:
Billionaire venture capitalist Reid Hoffman has put $8 million into the Democratic Party of Wisconsin over the past five weeks to help the party's gubernatorial nominee David Crowley in his race against Republican Tom Tiffany.
The LinkedIn co-founder gave $2 million on Sept. 24, $1 million on Oct. 2 and another $5 million in two installments on Oct. 5 and Oct. 20, according to Wisconsin campaign finance records. The rapid-fire checks are part of a last-minute spending spree by some of America's richest donors before Election Day.
In just the past week and a half, former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg gave Democratic Texas gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa $750,000, while Y Combinator co-founder Jessica Livingston chipped in another $150,000, state records show.
Bloomberg had already committed roughly $80 million to help Democrats this fall, much of it aimed at winning control of the House.
Meanwhile, PayPal co-founder Luke Nosek gave $500,000 on Tuesday to Judicial Fairness PAC, which supports conservative judicial candidates in Texas, according to Texas campaign finance records. The group had already received $2 million from Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, according to state records. Musk's roughly $475 million in disclosed political giving through late October makes him the cycle's biggest known individual donor.
The checks are landing in the middle of a final-week ad frenzy, with more than $1 billion now booked to air before Election Day, according to AdImpact. The 2026 cycle has already broken the record for political ad spending, with more than $11.2 billion spent or reserved, according to AdImpact. That's more than any previous presidential election cycle as well.
Hoffman has framed his own spending as a reluctant necessity.
"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote Friday on X. "And while others spend outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power, those of us who believe in the ideals of America cannot yield."
The House Majority PAC, the main super PAC working to elect House Democrats, has received $8.5 million from Hoffman this cycle, according to Federal Election Commission records.
In the past two weeks, the group has rolled out 13 ads related to disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. They total about $8.4 million in spending and nearly 719.4 million impressions, according to AdImpact. Until this month, it had not run a single Epstein-focused ad.
The spots have pushed Epstein into at least six battleground House races, accusing Republicans of helping block the release of government records related to Epstein or highlighting their ties to people in his orbit.
In Arizona's Second District, an ad called "Justice" attacked Republican Rep. Eli Crane over votes related to releasing the Epstein files and contributions from alleged Epstein associates. In Pennsylvania's Eighth District, ads called "Predators" and "Teacher" targeted Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan. And this week, an ad called "Exposed" went after Republican Rep. Mike Turner in Ohio's Tenth District over a contribution from an Epstein confidant and his record on releasing the files. All three races are tightly contested and could help determine control of the House in the next Congress.
There is no way to trace Hoffman's money to any particular ad because super PACs pool contributions from their donors. But the blitz comes with an obvious complication for Democrats: Hoffman's continued association with Epstein after the financier pleaded guilty in 2008 to sex offenses involving a minor.
Hoffman has acknowledged visiting Epstein's private island and meeting with him after the conviction. He has said the relationship grew out of fundraising for the MIT Media Lab and has repeatedly said he regrets continuing to meet with Epstein.
"My last interaction with Epstein was in 2015," Hoffman told Axios in 2019. "Still, by agreeing to participate in any fundraising activity where Epstein was present, I helped to repair his reputation and perpetuate injustice. For this, I am deeply regretful."
There is no allegation that Hoffman participated in Epstein's sex-trafficking crimes, but Republicans have nevertheless seized on the relationship. The Republican National Committee this week accused Democrats of hypocrisy for accepting Hoffman's money while using Epstein against GOP candidates.
"Democrats have no problem with money in politics so long as it benefits their own campaign," RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre told Fox News earlier this week.
And the attack has followed Hoffman's money into Wisconsin. In a new 15-second ad, Tiffany's campaign splices together clips of Crowley saying "Epstein" and "billionaires" before a narrator says they "are bankrolling David Crowley's campaign."

title: City of London chief tops UK Black Powerlist
titleJa: City of London chief tops UK Black Powerlist
summaryJa: Ian Thomas, who heads the City of London Corporation, tops the Black Powerlist in its 21st year.
bodyOriginal:
City of London chief tops UK Black Powerlist
- Published
Ian Thomas, chief executive of the City of London Corporation, has been named the UK's most influential Black Briton in this year's Black Powerlist awards.
The 57-year old is the first Black person to oversee the Square Mile's governing body in its more than 900-year history.
The City of London Corporation is an administrative body with responsibility for London's central financial district, headed by its own Lord Mayor.
Thomas tops the 2027 Black Powerlist, which recognises the most powerful people of African and Caribbean heritage in the UK.
The award body said he was "a respected public-service leader with over 30 years' experience in local government".
Other influential names in this year's top ten include entrepreneurs Emma Grede and Steven Bartlett, as well as actor and filmmaker Sir Idris Elba.
Comedian Sir Lenny Henry has also been recognised, with a Lifetime Achievement award, for co-founding Comic Relief, which has raised over £1.6bn since 1985.
Now in its 21st year, the Black Powerlist celebrates people who have broken through barriers to reach leadership roles, thereby inspiring future generations.
"It exists to show young people of African and Caribbean heritage what is possible, in fields they might never have considered," said Michael Eboda, the list's publisher.
Thomas said he secured the role at the head of the City of London Corporation in 2022 only following seven interviews and an election.
'When I started my journey in public service, I never, ever thought, [not] in a million years, that I'd be recognised in this way," he told the BBC.
'Discipline and respect'
As chief executive, he oversees around 5,000 staff with responsibilities including the City of London Police, 11,000 acres of open spaces such as Epping Forest and Hampstead Heath, and advocacy for the UK's financial and professional services sector.
Thomas was born in Sheffield to parents who made the city their home after leaving Jamaica as part of the Windrush generation.
"They worked incredibly hard and instilled that sense of discipline and respect, and that's the core of how I do business," he said of his upbringing.
Growing up, Thomas aspired to be a footballer and took part in trials alongside Alan Shearer.
Reflecting on his own change of direction, Thomas joked it was about "following dreams and if they don't come true… there's always something else".
Before joining the City of London Corporation, Thomas served as chief executive of the Royal Borough of Kingston upon Thames where he oversaw public services and a £1.2bn regeneration programme.
He was appointed a CBE in the 2019 New Year Honours in the wake of the Rotherham Abuse scandal for transforming children's services during his time as strategic director for children and young people at Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council.
Thomas replaces last year's incumbent, Afua Kyei, the Bank of England's chief financial officer and executive director, and is joined on this year's list by Comfort Ero, the President and chief executive of the International Crisis Group, who takes second place.

title: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months
titleJa: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months
summaryJa: The U.S. Department of the Treasury has announced new Series I bond rates through April 2027.
bodyOriginal:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury has announced new rates for Series I bonds.
Newly purchased I bonds will pay 5.51% annual interest from Nov. 1 through April 30, which is up from the 4.26% yield offered on purchases made through Oct. 31.
The new rate includes a variable portion of 4.08% based on inflation data, and a fixed portion of 1.40%. The fixed rate is up from 0.90% announced in April, and the highest since 2006.
Combined, the composite I bond rate is 5.51% after rounding, according to the Treasury.
Amid the post-pandemic inflation peak, the I bond rate hit a record high of 9.62% in May 2022, and investors poured millions into the government-backed, nearly risk-free asset.
As inflation cooled and I bond rates fell, many short-term investors redeemed I bonds. But investors could return as inflation pushes I bond rates back up, experts say.
"I bonds are a lot more attractive at this point," said David Enna, founder of Tipswatch.com, a website that tracks Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, and I bond rates.
I bonds are a lot more attractive at this point.David EnnaFounder of Tipswatch.com
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from an annual pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
In September, some higher inflation came from the Iran war, which pushed up gasoline and energy costs. President Donald Trump's tariffs, new artificial intelligence data centers and demand for travel have also added to rising prices, economists say.

title: Halloween gets pricier as chocolate costs climb — Hershey may feel the pinch
titleJa: Halloween gets pricier as chocolate costs climb — Hershey may feel the pinch
summaryJa: Higher cocoa and sugar prices are fueling above-average cost inflation for candy
bodyOriginal:
Halloween shopping got costlier this year as higher prices hit everything from the candy bowl to the pumpkin on your front porch.
It's not only rough on consumers, but may also hit companies like Hershey.
Americans are expected to spend $13.5 billion on Halloween, up from last year's record $13.1 billion, according to the National Retail Federation.
"Consumers continue to make Halloween a spending priority, but they are also approaching the season with affordability in mind," said Allison Zeller, NRF vice president of industry and consumer insights.
Inflation is rippling through everything from candy to costumes. Pumpkins are costlier too. The average retail price reached $5.36 this year, up 11% from September 2020, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Drought reduced yields by roughly 30% to 40% in parts of Texas, a major pumpkin-growing state.
Candy and chocolate
Candy remains one of the biggest expenses this Halloween and prices increases are running ahead of broader food inflation, though the rate of increase has slowed.
Candy and chewing gum prices were up 7.7% in September from a year earlier, according to the latest Consumer Price Index data. The sugar-and-sweets category increased 5.5% over the same period. Adverse weather, including the impact of El Niño, tightened the outlook for sugar supply. Unusually wet conditions disrupted Brazil's sugarcane harvest, while drought and other weather extremes affected production in other major growing regions.
"As Halloween swiftly approaches, candy stands out in the grocery store as one of the more expensive categories, relative to prices last year," food economist Richard Volpe wrote on LinkedIn. "In past years, this has left me swimming with candy," he added. "As I write this, Halloween is days away and I have a paltry three bags of candy sitting on my desk."
Nielsen IQ Early Market data showed Halloween candy sales down 11.7% through September 19. Four weeks later, the decline narrowed to 6.7%, with chocolate at -7.2% and confection at -5.3%, according to the report.
Chocolate so far has been the most vulnerable, especially after a disruption in cocoa supply in West Africa, which was hit by poor growing conditions in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. A potential El Niño and dry Harmattan trade winds could put pressure on the 2026-27 West African cocoa crop.
There was some relief in commodity markets after cocoa prices fell sharply from its historic highs, according to David Branch, sector manager at the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute.
But that drop has yet to translate into cheaper chocolates.
Wells Fargo Agri-Food estimates chocolate prices will be about 8% higher than last Halloween, with effective transaction prices rising roughly 5% to 8% after promotions. Much of the chocolate on shelves this Halloween was produced using cocoa bought six to 12 months earlier.
"The worst of the cocoa crisis has passed, but price relief hasn't reached store shelves yet," Branch told CNBC. "For chocolate manufacturers, the principal 2026 issue is no longer simply cocoa availability. It is the timing mismatch between falling futures, high-cost inventories, retailer negotiations, and consumer elasticity."
Halloween chocolate dollar sales were down 7.2% from a year earlier through the nine weeks ended Oct. 17, according to NIQ, with weakness in milk chocolate leading the decline.
NIQ estimates Halloween chocolate sales to be down $33.1 million from last year, with milk chocolate accounting for a $34.4 million decline. Dark chocolate, meanwhile, gained $2.3 million. Overall Halloween candy, gum and mint sales were down 6.7%.
To help juice sales, retailers are offering discounts — Walmart and Target have flash deals and heavy discounts on items from candy to Halloween costumes.
Candy shoppers, meanwhile, appear to be moving toward smaller packages. Small candy packs of nine ounces or less are up 24% in dollar terms and 14% in units, while every larger package size is declining, according to NIQ.
Wells Fargo expects shoppers to increasingly favor value packs and alternatives that use less cocoa, including gummies, sour candy, wafers and caramel.
"Consumers will continue buying candy, but shopping baskets are likely to contain fewer chocolate pieces, more value packs, and a greater share of gummies, sour products, wafers, caramel, and other lower-cocoa alternatives," Branch said.
Hershey stock was rising on Friday as consumers ditched AI stocks for safer consumer staples. But analysts see trouble brewing for the candy maker.
The company, which reported third quarter results on Thursday, lowered its 2026 organic sales growth forecast to 3% (from 3%-3.5%). That implies "flattish" organic growth in the fourth quarter, according to Jefferies analyst Scott Marks
Hershey's commentary was "incrementally cautious," he added in a note, saying "consumer and cost pressures" are weighing on the near-term outlook.
"We're looking at areas like in convenience as you see a consumer that's under pressure to give more value and drive pricing through bespoke promotions versus overall price decreases," Hershey CEO Kirk Tanner told analysts on an earnings call.
Marks cut his price target on the stock to $170, joining cuts at brokerages such as DA Davidson, BNP Paribas, Bernstein and Deutsche Bank. Consensus estimates for 2027 earnings fell 3.7% to $9.49 a share, according to FactSet.
CNBC's Alex Harring contributed to the reporting.

title: Swiss central bank posts bumper $23bn profit as gold, foreign assets soar
titleJa: Swiss central bank posts bumper $23bn profit as gold, foreign assets soar
summaryJa: Unlike other major central banks, the Swiss National Bank has a significant equity portfolio.
bodyOriginal:
The Swiss National Bank said Friday that it made a profit of 19.1 billion Swiss francs ($23.3 billion) on its investments in the third quarter, driven by its gold and foreign currency holdings.
It brought the central bank's year-to-date profit up to 44.2 billion francs, the equivalent of around $53.8 billion, raising the prospect of a payout to Swiss federal and local governments at the end of the year.
But the overall profit in the third quarter of 2026 marked a year-on-year decline of almost 32%.
Profit and loss recorded in the SNB's quarterly accounting updates consists of interest income, dividends, and valuation adjustments resulting from exchange rate movements and market price changes.
The Swiss franc rose around 12% against the U.S. dollar in 2025, having been lifted by investors flocking to the safe-haven currency in the wake of U.S. President Donald Trump's tariff announcements.
So far this year, it has lost around 3.6% versus the greenback.
Profit drivers
In the third quarter of 2025, the SNB saw a 14.3-billion-franc net gain on gold, compared to a net gain on gold of 7.6 billion francs in the three months to September.
The yellow metal saw a record-smashing rally in 2025, with its value surging by around 66% over the course of 2025. But its trajectory has been far more volatile in 2026, and the metal has fallen in value by more than 7% since the start of the year.
Profit on the SNB's foreign currency positions, which include investments in international equities, reached 11.6 billion francs, marking a year-on-year decline of around 15%.
Most of the SNB's foreign currency reserves are held in financial assets denominated in foreign currencies, as opposed to hard currency holdings. It also has a smaller Swiss franc bond portfolio.
At the end of the third quarter, 61% of its foreign currency reserves were allocated to government bonds, including deposits with central banks and the Bank for International Settlements, while 28% were invested in equities and 11% in other bonds.
In terms of currency exposure, 39% of the portfolio was denominated in euros and 37% in U.S. dollars. Japanese yen and British pound exposure accounted for 7% and 6%, respectively.
The SNB's stocks portfolio
The SNB's large equity portfolio makes it unusual compared to other major central banks like the U.S. Federal Reserve and the Bank of England, which do not typically invest directly in equity markets.
However, the SNB is a passive investor, and therefore does not engage in equity selection. Its stock holdings are based on a benchmark index composed of international stock indexes, with its portfolio mostly made up of shares of mid- and large-cap companies in developed markets.
Its profits are mostly distributed to Switzerland's federal and local governments, with shareholders receiving a dividend if its equity capital is large enough. If the investments generate a loss, the SNB may be unable to make payouts.
Despite the country benefiting from a strong investment performance, however, the SNB's investments are not focused on achieving the highest possible return.
"For a conventional company, profits are an important prerequisite for long-term success. The SNB's goal, by contrast, is not to generate profit," it says on its website. "It has another mandate: It must ensure price stability in Switzerland, while taking due account of economic developments."
"The monetary policy mandate always has highest priority. The SNB can thus find itself having to take monetary policy decisions that may have a negative impact on its annual result."
Unlike many other major central banks, the SNB's monetary policy mandate allows it to use interest rates and exchange rates to achieve price stability, and it will use measures to influence the exchange rate if deemed necessary.
The SNB's inflation target also makes it an outlier among its international peers, with its target range for inflation being 0% to 2%.

title: The big questions remaining after Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO prospectus
titleJa: The big questions remaining after Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO prospectus
summaryJa: Uncertainties remain ahead of one of the most hotly anticipated IPOs in history.
bodyOriginal:
This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here.
Anthropic's over 300 page S-1 filing earlier this week contained a lot of information. It was the most comprehensive public statement to date about how a pure-play AI lab makes its money.
After the prospectus went live on Monday, my U.S.-based colleagues and I went through it with a fine-tooth comb, detailing everything from revenue and risks to competitors and computing costs.
The filing also revealed that CEO Dario Amodei and his six co-founders each own over 200 million shares, which could be worth billions if Anthropic hits the over $1 trillion valuation it's expected to.
But despite all the nuggets, a few big questions remain.
Revenue
Anthropic reported its cost of revenue as $2.38 billion in the first half of 2026, booking $16.29 billion in revenue during the same period and implying a gross margin of 85%.
Violeta Todorova, senior research analyst at Leverage Shares, told CNBC that the first-half revenue compared with just $1.16 billion in the first half of 2025, and asked whether it could grow to "keep pace with expectations."
"It is unclear how much it costs to generate each additional dollar of revenue as computing demand increases," she said.
But Anthropic's meteoric revenue growth slowed in the third quarter. It grew approximately 144% in the second quarter compared to the first quarter, followed by roughly 47% in the third quarter.
"What the prospectus didn't tell us is management's expectations around the sequential slowdown in the growth rate," said Michael Field, chief equity strategist at Morningstar.
Compute
"Substantially all of cost of revenue" is associated with compute and infrastructure costs, the filing states. It also says that operating margin and adjusted operating margin are expected to "fluctuate over time, particularly in periods when substantial incremental compute is delivered to us and we incur the associated expenses."
"Investors can see compute falling as a share of revenue, but not how much of the forward commitment is earmarked for training the next generation of models versus serving customers," Nick Patience, AI lead at the Futurum Group, told CNBC. "That split dictates future margins."
Questions also remain around whether compute costs can keep falling faster than commitments grow and if Anthropic can secure enough capacity to serve customers, he added.
Regarding demand across the AI and hyperscaler sector outstripping supply, the prospectus says that it had previously sought "quantities of compute from [cloud service providers] in excess of what those partners were willing to provide."
Later it says: "We have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us."
Pricing and control
Anthropic's structure as a public benefit corporation raises questions, too. Seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, have special voting power through a single Class F share equal to 50.1% of total voting power over matters brought to a shareholder vote.
Anthropic describes its capital and corporate governance structure as having "no direct public company precedent," in the filing.
"We also know now that management plans a series of different class share issues," said Morningstar's Field. "But what we don't know is whether investors will be fine with the lack of control implied, or will this impact the share price. Something we won't know until the shares start trading."
And finally the trillion-dollar question: the IPO valuation that Anthropic targets. The AI lab is keeping schtum about that, for now. It says simply it will be "determined by negotiations among us, the selling stockholders, and the representatives."
Given analyst estimates range between $1 trillion and $2 trillion, it will be a huge market event. If it's at the higher end of the range, it could bring back some of the swagger the AI sector has lost in recent weeks. If on the lower end, things could get ugly.
News edit
Apple on Wednesday announced its first laptop with a touchscreen, which it's calling MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display.
SK Hynix's shares rose after the company reported record quarterly profit that sharply beat estimates, and announced over $25 billion in dividends and buybacks.
Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices said they will invest a total of $4 billion in Meta after the social media giant announced plans to raise $95 billion to support its investments in AI infrastructure.
Microsoft said Monday that it's offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees as it strives to balance a costly AI infrastructure build-out with capital efficiency.
SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy graphics processing units, or GPUs, used to power AI systems, Elon Musk said on Sunday.
One more thing
Anthropic's S-1 was a trove of company intel, but one figure really caught my eye. The AI lab has more cash than almost every company in the U.S. And, as my colleague Leslie Picker writes, never before has a company gone public with anywhere near that much.

What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack
Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, has been hit by a $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack - thought to be the biggest in history.

title: Chevron and Exxon beat earnings expectations as refining profits soar on high diesel fuel prices
titleJa: Chevron and Exxon beat earnings expectations as refining profits soar on high diesel fuel prices
summaryJa: Diesel prices have surged globally as Ukraine and Iran have bombed refineries in Russia and the Middle East.
bodyOriginal:
Chevron and ExxonMobil on Friday reported profits that surged in the third quarter, as their U.S. refineries ran at full capacity to take advantage of high diesel fuel prices.
Chevron's net income surged nearly 200% to $9.9 billion, or $5.06 a share, compared to $3.5 billion, or $1.82 a share, in the same period last year. When adjusted for one-time items, it reported earnings of $5.28 per share, soundly beating Wall Street's expectations of $4.89.
Diesel prices have surged globally as Ukraine and Iran have bombed refineries in Russia and the Middle East. U.S. refiners have ramped up production to fill the supply gap.
ExxonMobil's profits doubled to $15.4 billion, or $3.72 a share, compared to $7.5 billion, or $1.76 a share, in the same period in 2025. When adjusted for one-time items, it posted earnings of $4.23 a share, beating the Street's expectations.
Chevron shares are up about 2% in premarket trading, while Exxon is trading about 1.5% higher.
Here's how Chevron and Exxon did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
- Chevron's earnings per share: $5.28 adjusted, vs. $4.89 expected
- Chevron's revenue: $67.8 billion, vs. $61.6 billion expected
- Exxon's earnings per share: $4.23 adjusted, vs. $4.08 expected
- Exxon's revenue: $113.2 billion, vs. $103.1 billion expected
Chevron's U.S. refineries processed record amounts of crude oil at just above 1 million barrels per day, as the facilities ran at 98% capacity. Diesel and jet fuel yields rose more than 10%, the company said.
Exxon's Gulf Coast refineries operated at 100% utilization with the second-highest diesel production on record at those facilities, the company said.

Chevron's output actually declined slightly to 3.9 million barrels per day compared to about 4 million bpd in the same period last year. The decline was in its international segment due in part to the conflict in the Middle East, while output was largely flat in the U.S. year over year.
Exxon has produced about 4.5 million bpd this year, a more than 2% decline from nearly 4.7 million during the first nine months of 2025.

title: Musk and Zuckerberg echo Trump's push to rebrand AI as 'super intelligence' on earnings calls. Others did not
titleJa: Musk and Zuckerberg echo Trump's push to rebrand AI as 'super intelligence' on earnings calls. Others did not
summaryJa: Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX adopted President Trump's preferred "super intelligence" term on their third-quarter earnings calls.
bodyOriginal:
A month after President Donald Trump ordered that the term "super intelligence" replace artificial intelligence within executive branch departments and agencies, his leading tech allies — Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg — followed suit on earnings calls. Their fellow tech CEOs were less eager to do the same.
Trump's declaration took place on Sept. 29, while he was hosting an AI luncheon at the White House for industry leaders. At the time, he was working to ensure the growth of AI in the U.S. with limited regulations. The president this week announced on Truth Social that he's banning the use of AI or artificial intelligence in "all relevant documents" and "everything else."
SpaceX and Tesla adhered to Trump's wishes on earnings calls last week after Musk, earlier in October, changed the name of his rocket company's AI division to SpaceXSI. Speaking on Tesla's call about his work on humanoid robots, Musk said, "Some of them look very impressive, but they're not really using any kind of advanced AI or SI."
Zuckerberg was equally compliant on Meta's earnings call on Oct. 21, emphasizing his company's "goal of delivering personal superintelligence to everyone." However, Meta was already using the term, having created a unit called Meta Superintelligence Labs last year.
While Musk and Zuckerberg have been perhaps the fiercest supporters of the Trump administration among tech's CEOs, they're by no means outliers. Leaders of all the tech giants have contributed to Trump's inauguration festivities or his plan for the White House ballroom, and some have been intentional about getting rid of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs that the president opposed.
But for now at least, they're holding out when it comes to eliminating the term AI.
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy peppered his call with use of AI on Thursday, uttering the acronym well over a dozen times in his introductory remarks. A day earlier, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said one of the company's three points of focus is "designing AI to empower people." And Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai was seconds into his quarterly earnings commentary when he said the search giant's "AI investments are driving increased usage and overall user growth."
Trump's attempted rebrand comes just ahead of the midterm elections next week, with the Republican Party in jeopardy of losing control of both the House and Senate. Trump's job approval has been dropping and his economic approval rating just hit an all-time low, according to the latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey released last week.
'Real-world outcomes'
That's not to suggest tech execs sticking with "AI" on this week's earnings calls are openly defying the president. Trump's preferred term is seeping into other correspondence and documents. Microsoft's annual report filed last week included eight mentions of super intelligence, starting at the top of the letter to shareholders.
"For Microsoft, the central question as we enter this Super Intelligence era is not just how big the opportunity becomes, but how we deliver the real-world outcomes that every country, community, and company demands and deserves," Nadella wrote.
IBM CEO Arvind Krishna, who didn't attend Trump's September lunch, used SI alongside AI during his company's earnings call last week. Krishna said, "technology innovation in both hybrid infrastructure and super intelligence is leading to better business performance," adding that IBM is advancing as a "software-led hybrid cloud and AI platform company."
Lip-Bu Tan, CEO of chipmaker Intel, said on Thursday the supply shortage the chip industry is navigating has been "driven by the unprecedented demand for super intelligence."
Some in the tech industry have been explicit in their support of Trump's terminology ahead of their forthcoming earnings reports next month.
Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora repeatedly referred to SI on CNBC, and posted on X on Sept. 30, "The meeting at the WH on SI was an epic moment."
Then there's Nvidia's Jensen Huang, who runs the world's most valuable company and the chipmaker that's powered much of the AI boom. Along with Musk and Zuckerberg, Huang has been one of Trump's most vocal supporters in tech and the president's top ally on the AI safety debate.
Like Arora, Huang took to X after last month's AI meeting to praise the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence."
"Super Intelligence offers an extraordinary opportunity to advance discovery, productivity, security, health, and prosperity," Huang wrote. "The future of Super Intelligence will be shaped not only by what it can do, but by the confidence it earns."

title: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
titleJa: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
summaryJa: The government is under pressure to set out a path to greater defence spending, as ministers unveil plans to boost UK firms.
bodyOriginal:
Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
- Published
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has denied "kicking the can down the road" over how much the UK spends on defence.
The government has faced criticism for not setting out a pathway at Wednesday's Budget to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
Streeting is at odds with MPs on the Commons defence committee over the issue.
It comes as Chancellor John Healey and Streeting announce that foreign firms which are awarded defence contracts of more than £50m will need to invest an equal value back into the UK.
Under the new investment rules, described as an "offset strategy", these companies will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.
The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said. Healey and Streeting will unveil the policy on a visit to UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow later.
Countries including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the government said.
While ministers hope the rules increase investment in Britain's defence industry, they appear designed to do so in a politically palatable way rather than committing to spending cuts.
Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the cross-party Commons defence committee, said on Wednesday that decisions had been "kicked into the long grass" to next year's government spending review, rather than announced in the Budget.
He warned that without building capabilities now, "we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict".
Streeting hit back at these comments as "unfair" and "unfounded".
Speaking on Thursday, Dhesi said the committee stands by its criticism.
"We had hoped to see that the chancellor would set out a precise pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030," Dhesi told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
"But instead some of those key decisions on defence have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review."
He praised the government for plugging a £4.7bn hole in the Defence Investment Plan in the Budget, through asking government departments to cut their capital budgets by 1%.
Responding on Thursday, Streeting told Today: "I like Tan very much, he's a friend and I respect him, but I strongly disagree with him.
"And I don't think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we're funding right now."
Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules, aiming to create "bang for the British buck", would help achieve this target given increasing defence spending "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".
He said waiting for the spending review, which does not have a fixed date and could come in the second half of 2027, was "the right thing to do" so ministers can look at "spending in the round".
He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be".
"There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.
Defence analysts have questioned the government's ability to deliver on its 2030 target and the Nato-wide target of 3.5% by 2035. UK defence spending is at an estimated 2.6% of GDP this year.
Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional £10bn annually to reach its targets.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%".
Healey resigned as then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June over not spending enough on defence.
In the Budget, Healey said the UK was negotiating with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to set up an international bank - the Multilateral Defence Mechanism - to boost defence investment and joint procurement.
But Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said this amounted to "turning to borrowing at a time when the national debt is over £3 trillion".
"The answer is not more borrowing – it's to cut welfare to fund defence," he said.

title: Wall Street braces for Democratic gains as 2026 midterm election nears
titleJa: Wall Street braces for Democratic gains as 2026 midterm election nears
summaryJa: Investors are preparing for a blue wave in the midterm election on Tuesday that will determine who controls Congress for the remainder of President Trump's term.
bodyOriginal:
Investors expect a blue wave in next week's midterm election, as Democrats surge in polls and President Donald Trump's approval rating remains low.
Public polling suggests Democrats are likely to take control of the House of Representatives, and analysts who parse what politics means for investors are in overdrive to tell their clients how to prepare for what Congress will look like after the Tuesday election.
Concern about the spending plans and priorities of a Democratic-controlled Congress permeates analyst reports reviewed by CNBC. But because Trump has another two years of his presidency, a divided government would likely create gridlock that would prevent congressional leadership in opposition to the president from getting much done, analysts are advising their clients.
Most analysts believe Democrats are also within striking distance of a Senate majority, though that outcome is significantly less likely than a House flip according to the polls. Next Tuesday's elections will determine which party controls both chambers of Congress for the remainder of Trump's presidency, after two years of full Republican control.
Divided government typically makes must-pass legislation, like government funding and raising the debt ceiling, harder to enact. A debt ceiling standoff — or first-ever default on federal debt — could be particularly damaging.
Wall Street watchers are also expecting Democrats to try to advance an ambitious and expensive agenda should they gain control of Congress. An Oct. 29 report from Piper Sandler analyzing Congressional Budget Office data projected that policy proposals from Democrats "would add $5 trillion to the deficit over the coming decade." The analysis assumes repeals of Trump's tariffs and reversing cuts to Medicaid, nutrition programs and Affordable Care Act subsidies.
Major policy swings — and big spending packages — become less likely as a divided government is unlikely to agree on issues. That's a dynamic the market typically enjoys. Trump's veto power would effectively block major Democratic policies from becoming law.
"A blue House is the obvious consensus base case," Wolfe Research said in an Oct. 27 report. The firm surveyed 138 investors and found 96% of those polled believed Democrats would prevail in House control.
"The scale of polling error that would be required for Republicans to retain House control would be unprecedented in modern history, well above the polling error in the famously bad 2020 cycle," Wolfe wrote.
Wolfe is less bullish on a Democratic Senate, though investors clearly see a possibility that Democrats regain control of both chambers of Congress.
Fifty-eight percent of investors the firm surveyed believed Democrats would gain control of the Senate, while 42% believed Republicans would retain control of the chamber. The investors surveyed were more bullish than Wolfe itself, which puts the chances of a Democratic Senate at 49%.
Other analysts are largely coalescing around the potential for a good night for Democrats.
"A blue wave scenario has become our base case," an Oct. 20 report from TD Securities reads. An Oct. 23 Raymond James report says "Democrats are in a solid position to win a majority in the House of Representatives and are increasingly likely to win enough seats to capture a Senate majority."
Even if Democrats sweep both chambers, protracted battles could still play out as Republicans maintain the White House and the Senate must still surpass the 60-vote filibuster threshold.
Democrats winning control of the Senate could allay concerns about the Federal Reserve's independence from Trump, TD predicted.
That's because any new Fed members would need to be confirmed by the Senate, which would be unlikely to support a nominee who wouldn't support the central bank charting its own course.
Democrats are also expected to investigate companies that have done business with the Trump administration should they win control of a chamber. The majority party in Congress holds subpoena power on committees. Some Democrats have already telegraphed their investigative priorities ahead of the election.
The debt ceiling is likely the most critical sticking point for the economy that lawmakers will need to address during the next Congress, unless Republicans raise it during the lame-duck session between the election and the start of the next Congress in January. The Bipartisan Policy Center expects the U.S. will reach the so-called X-date — the point at which Treasury runs out of cash under the debt ceiling — between late-winter and mid-summer 2027.
"While negotiations around the debt ceiling may come down to the wire, a Democratic Congress would make it slightly more likely that a bill is passed than a divided Congress," TD said.
If Congress does not raise the debt ceiling by the X-date, the U.S. could default on its debt, causing catastrophic economic consequences.
Democrats, should they control one slice of government, are expected to demand concessions from Republicans in exchange for their votes to raise the debt ceiling. That sets up a potential standoff, which analysts note Republicans could avoid if they lose next week and raise the debt ceiling during the lame duck.
"[R]aising the debt limit before January could substantially reduce leverage Democrats have over healthcare, Medicaid, SNAP, and broader domestic spending priorities in the next Congress," Raymond James told its clients.

summaryJa: Nicola Shaw, who has led the company since 2022, will step down in January, it is announced.
bodyOriginal:
Yorkshire Water boss resigns after firm downgraded
- Published
Yorkshire Water's chief executive has announced she is to step down, just 24 hours after the company was given the lowest possible environmental rating by the Environment Agency
Nicola Shaw, who has led the firm since 2022, will leave the role on 1 January to be replaced by Nicola Medalova, a chartered environmental health officer who previously worked for the National Grid.
In a statement on Friday, Shaw said it had been a "privilege" to lead the company but that it was "the right time" to leave her post.
Shaw has faced criticism in recent years, including for taking £1.9m in undisclosed payments between 2023 and 2026, while the company has come under scrutiny for its performance.
The payments were made by Yorkshire Water's parent company, Kelda Holdings, for what the firm said was for "investor engagement" and "financial oversight".
On Thursday, the Environment Agency gave the firm one star out of four - its lowest possible rating - meaning Yorkshire Water was classed as a "poorly performing company".
The EA said Yorkshire Water was responsible for 260 pollution incidents in 2025, which was its highest total since 2011.
In 2024, Ofwat announced it was fining the company £47m for historic sewage leaks.
'Extremely proud'
In her statement, Shaw said: "It has been a privilege to lead Yorkshire Water and serve the people of Yorkshire.
"Although there remains a huge amount of work to do, I am extremely proud of what our colleagues have achieved, putting the business on a stronger footing for delivery across all aspects of its work."
Yorkshire Water said Medalova would join the company on Monday as part of a transition period before assuming the chief executive officer role full time in the new year.
She said: "I am delighted to be joining Yorkshire Water and grateful to the Board for the opportunity to lead the business through its next chapter.
"Yorkshire Water faces huge challenges but also great opportunities for continued improvement and I look forward to working with Nicola Shaw, the leadership team and colleagues across the business as I get up to speed."
In December last year Shaw said "not being transparent" about receiving £1.3m in shareholder-funded payments across two instalments had been a "mistake", but had insisted those amounts were "not for me to decide".
She received a further £660,000 earlier this year. Ofwat said the payments were not performance-related.
The previously undisclosed payments had come to light the previous August when the government banned Yorkshire Water and five other water companies from paying "unfair" bonuses to bosses.
